title: Gold Imports Plunge 57% as Festive Season Tests India's Golden Appetite
excerpt: August gold imports fell to $2.3 billion from $5.4 billion a year ago — and jewellers say the festive season will reshape, not erase, India's gold habit.
body:
• India's gold imports plunged 57% in August to $2.3 billion from $5.4 billion a year earlier, government trade data showed — one of the steepest monthly drops in recent years and a major reason the trade deficit narrowed.
  • The collapse follows Prime Minister Narendra Modi's appeal earlier this year urging Indians to refrain from buying gold for a year to protect foreign exchange reserves as the West Asia crisis pressures the rupee.
  • Jewellery industry leaders say the festive season is more likely to bring a shift in buying behaviour than a demand collapse, with exchange-led purchases — old gold traded in for new jewellery — expected to dominate.
  • Senco Gold told CNBC TV18 the festive rush is "just getting started" and expects to cross its 200-store milestone by December, signalling confidence despite the import slump.

India bought $3.1 billion less gold in August than it did a year ago. Gold imports plunged 57% to $2.3 billion from $5.4 billion in August 2025, according to trade data released on Tuesday — a dramatic pullback that did much of the work in narrowing India's trade deficit for the month.

The timing is hard to miss. The slump comes after Prime Minister Narendra Modi's appeal earlier this year asking Indians to refrain from buying gold for a year to protect foreign exchange reserves. The request, made as the West Asia crisis sent oil prices surging and pressured the rupee, put the country's most culturally loaded purchase at the centre of economic policy.

India is the world's second-largest gold consumer and imports nearly all of its demand. In 2025-26, the country's gold import bill hit an all-time high of $71.98 billion — up more than 24% — even as physical volumes fell nearly 5% to roughly 721 tonnes, reflecting elevated global prices. When the Prime Minister spoke, shares of jewellery makers including Titan, Senco Gold and Kalyan Jewellers fell between 6% and 8% in a single session on fears the government might sharply raise import duties to curb imports.

A behavioural shift, not a collapse

Now, with the festive season underway, the jewellery industry is reading the tea leaves — and its verdict is that Modi's message may change how Indians buy gold more than how much they buy.

"What we expect over the coming quarters is not a contraction in demand so much as a shift in how that demand is met," said M.P. Ahammad, chairman of Malabar Group, who expects exchange-led purchases — consumers trading old gold for new jewellery instead of making fresh bullion-heavy buys — to become the dominant trend as buyers turn value-conscious amid elevated prices and policy messaging around cutting imports.

"What we expect over the coming quarters is not a contraction in demand so much as a shift in how that demand is met."

— M.P. Ahammad, Chairman, Malabar Group

Varghese Alukkas, managing director of Jos Alukkas, drew a distinction between segments: the investment-led buyer is more vulnerable to messaging of this kind than the jewellery buyer. "Jewellery buying for occasions has historically been more resilient," he said. Joy Alukkas chairman Dr Joy Alukkas echoed the point, saying Indian gold consumption remains deeply rooted in tradition, especially during weddings and festivals — commentary may shift timing or push buyers toward lighter designs, but the emotional and cultural demand stays.

Retailers still betting on the season

The organised trade is acting like the festival calendar matters more than the policy calendar. Senco Gold told CNBC TV18 that the festive rush is "just getting started" and that it expects to cross its 200-store milestone by December — an expansion plan that would be hard to justify if the industry expected demand to stay depressed.

Why it matters beyond the trade data

Gold sits at an unusual intersection in India: a cultural necessity, a household savings vehicle, and one of the largest single items on the import bill. Every surge in festive buying can widen the trade deficit and add pressure on the rupee — which fell to a more-than-one-month low this week. The August import collapse shows the Prime Minister's appeal, combined with high prices, is having a real effect on the trade account. Whether the festive season reverses it — or simply reshapes it into exchanged old gold — will be visible in the next two months of data.
